# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
A full-charge baseline using one solvent/catalyst pair, high-temperature reaction hold, then seeded controlled cooling and cold aging should produce measurable target crystals. I expect catalyst and solvent identity to dominate reaction yield/selectivity, while slower cooling and moderate seed dose should reduce fines relative to an unseeded rapid cool. This first batch is exploratory; I will change the material pair if conversion/selectivity are poor, and change thermal/seeding history if reaction metrics are adequate but recovery or fines fail.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only for reaction feasibility]
C0/S0 and C1/S0 at 370 K for 1 h both give complete conversion and substantial target formation; C1/S0 is numerically better in final target yield/selectivity (events runner-operation-0014, runner-operation-0026). Both final crystal purities are about 0.98 and overall crystal recovery about 0.46–0.47, so upstream chemistry and purity are not the present constraint. One noisy comparison does not establish a catalyst effect.

## H2 [disconfirmed in tested scope]
Moving the 0.05 g seed addition from before cooling to 330 K and using staged 330→300→280 K cooling did not materially solve fines: particle-size readings remained about 0.81 fines (runner-operation-0011 versus runner-operation-0023), and final assays were about 0.81–0.83 (runner-operation-0014, runner-operation-0026). The size index rose numerically, but uncertainty and catalyst confounding preclude a firm timing effect.

## H3 [tentative; prospective]
A temperature-cycle ripening treatment—cold precipitation, partial reheating near 315 K, warm hold, then slow recooling—may dissolve the smallest crystals and lower the number fraction below 20 µm. Next batch will test this while continuing material screening. I will abandon this explanation if fines remain near 0.8 after a substantive reheat/recool cycle.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only for reaction feasibility]
All tested material pairs have produced high conversion and high final crystal purity, but target selectivity/yield differ. C1/S0 remains the best observed reaction/recovery combination (runner-operation-0026). Single-batch solvent comparisons are confounded by harvest temperature and should not be ranked causally yet.

## H2 [rejected in tested scope]
A 280→315→280 K cycle worsened fines to about 0.97 and reduced recovery (runner-operation-0039), contrary to the proposed ripening benefit. Possible renewed nucleation or catalyst confounding remains, but I will not repeat this cycle.

## H3 [tentative, narrowed]
Stopping crystallization warmer lowers supersaturation and appears capable of reducing fines: 310–320 K batches gave intermediate fines around 0.68–0.74 (runner-operation-0050, runner-operation-0061), compared with about 0.81–0.97 at 280 K. Solvent-S3 is an opposing observation (about 0.92 fines even at 325 K; runner-operation-0072), so material identity also matters. Next test returns to C1/S0 and harvests at 325 K; prediction is lower recovery than batch 2 but materially fewer fines, potentially near the 0.50 limit.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
C1/S0 reproducibly gives complete conversion, final reaction yield around 0.63–0.66, and crystal purity above 0.97 (runner-operation-0026, runner-operation-0083, runner-operation-0092). It is the preferred upstream pair unless a later material gives a clear constrained advantage.

## H2 [rejected]
Simple warm stopping is not monotonically associated with fewer fines. C1/S0 harvested at 325 K gave about 0.98 fines (runner-operation-0083), opposing the earlier cross-material trend. Harvest temperature comparisons across solvents were confounded.

## H3 [unresolved]
Removing seed did not solve fines: unseeded C1/S0 at 310 K still gave about 0.87 fines (runner-operation-0092). Thus purchased seed is not the sole source of small-particle counts.

## H4 [tentative; prospective]
The consistently small size indices suggest insufficient growth time rather than only excessive supersaturation. I will test a long isothermal controlled hold after seeded cooling, using repeated control advances at 300 K. Prediction: size index rises and fines fall versus short-hold C1/S0 batches; if not, I will instead test process dilution/loading.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
C1/S0 remains the most reproducible high-conversion, high-purity upstream choice; short processes give final reaction yield near 0.63–0.66. Long thermal exposure is harmful.

## H2 [rejected]
A 16 h controlled hold at 300 K did not grow out fines; it produced essentially all-fines material and strong degradation/byproduct formation (runner-operation-0108). A half-loading unseeded batch also remained essentially all fines (runner-operation-0117), so simple dilution is not a solution.

## H3 [unresolved]
No completed batch yet meets the fines constraint. The best numerical fines result is batch 5 (about 0.68 at S2/C1 and 320 K; runner-operation-0061), but it is not compliant. Shorter thermal histories outperform prolonged holds on reaction quality.

## H4 [tentative; prospective]
Because the seed dose is fixed at a small maximum and all d50 indices remain low, a deeper single slow cool may deposit more mass on existing particles and increase size enough to offset additional nucleation. Next test uses C1/S0, seed at 330 K, one 4 h cool to 250 K, and immediate filtration. If fines worsen, the final batch will instead revisit the numerically best S2 warm-harvest condition.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
C1/S0 is the strongest observed upstream pair for unconstrained recovery, reaching crystal yield about 0.57 with high purity under deep cooling, but its fines remain about 0.81 (runner-operation-0128). It is not recommendable under the stated quality constraint.

## H2 [supported for the tested recipe]
Solvent-S2 combined with C1 and a warm, narrow seeded crystallization window (335 K pre-cool, 0.05 g seed, then 325 K for 4 h) achieved the only demonstrated compliant particle distribution: final fines about 0.409, purity about 0.994, and overall crystal yield about 0.278 (runner-operation-0138). This substantially improves on the same material pair harvested at 320 K, which had higher numerical recovery (~0.294) but noncompliant fines (~0.679; runner-operation-0061). The comparison is consistent with a sharp nucleation threshold between 325 and 320 K for S2, though two batches do not establish exact boundary or repeatability.

## H3 [rejected approaches]
The tested reheat/recool cycle, prolonged 300 K hold, and half-loading unseeded process all failed to reduce fines and sometimes increased degradation (runner-operation-0039, runner-operation-0108, runner-operation-0117).

## Decision
Recommend lifecycle batch 12 because it is the only completed batch meeting both purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50, and it provides meaningful recovery above the feasibility target. The main uncertainty is replication near the apparent 320–325 K particle-quality boundary; a future study should replicate batch 12 and map this interval before claiming robust scale-up.

K1.report:
## Scope and public background

This is a bounded synthetic benchmark, not a model of named real chemicals. Catalysts C0–C3 and solvents S0–S3 are anonymous; their indices carry no public chemical meaning. The limiting reagent is likewise anonymous, so mechanistic statements below concern observed process behavior, not molecular identities.

The public objective was to maximize seed-excluded crystal recovery subject to crystal purity ≥0.80 and a number fraction below 20 µm ≤0.50. Public definitions were:

- `crystal_yield` = moles of target product in recovered solids, excluding purchased seed, divided by initial reagent moles, clipped to [0,1].
- `crystal_size` = min(number-weighted d50/250 µm, 1).
- `crystal_fines_fraction` = number fraction below 20 µm.

Thus a useful conceptual decomposition is

`overall crystal yield ≈ chemical target yield × crystallization/separation recovery`,

but this is an interpretive factorization, not a separately validated kinetic law. High conversion alone cannot guarantee high crystal recovery because selectivity, degradation, solubility, nucleation, growth and separation intervene.

Final-assay nominal noise scales were 0.006 for reaction yield, 0.010 for selectivity and crystal yield/purity, 0.025 for crystal size, and 0.018 for CSD quality and fines. Particle-size measurements had nominal noise 0.015 for their outputs. Process-proxy uncertainty is additional. There were no exact recipe replicates, so causal conclusions are limited.

## Experimental domain

Twelve completed batches were assayed. Most used 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L solvent and 0.005 mol catalyst, with reaction heating near 370 K for 3600 s. Batch 10 alone used 0.020 mol reagent and 0.0025 mol catalyst. Crystallization histories varied in solvent, catalyst, seed use, terminal temperature, holding time and temperature cycling. Seeded batches used 0.05 g seed. All reported values below are actual final-assay observations.

## Actual observations

### Upstream material and reaction behavior

C1/S0 was the most consistently productive upstream combination in the explored short processes:

- Batch 2: conversion 1.000, reaction yield 0.649, selectivity 0.661, crystal yield 0.475 and purity 0.983.
- Batch 7: conversion 1.000, reaction yield 0.655, selectivity 0.629, crystal yield 0.220 and purity 0.970.
- Batch 8: conversion 1.000, reaction yield 0.631, selectivity 0.639, crystal yield 0.353 and purity 0.974.
- Batch 11: conversion 0.999, reaction yield 0.647, selectivity 0.666, crystal yield 0.566 and purity 0.995.

The differences in crystal yield among these batches arose despite similar reaction outputs, demonstrating strong downstream process-history dependence.

Other observed material combinations were:

- C0/S0, batch 1: reaction yield 0.604, selectivity 0.606, crystal yield 0.460, purity 0.979.
- C2/S0 with a temperature cycle, batch 3: reaction yield 0.537, selectivity 0.538, crystal yield 0.366, purity 0.979.
- C1/S1, batch 4: reaction yield 0.590, selectivity 0.604, crystal yield 0.362, purity 1.000.
- C1/S2, batch 5: reaction yield 0.538, selectivity 0.544, crystal yield 0.294, purity 0.977.
- C1/S3, batch 6: reaction yield 0.525, selectivity 0.523, crystal yield 0.158, purity 0.992.
- C1/S2, batch 12: reaction yield 0.528, selectivity 0.523, crystal yield 0.278, purity 0.994.

These observations suggest C1/S0 favors upstream target formation relative to the tested C1/S1–S3 cases. However, solvent comparisons were not run under a complete factorial design, and crystallization histories differed, so a pure solvent effect cannot be separated quantitatively. Likewise, batch 3 does not isolate a C2 catalyst effect because its reheat/recool history was unique.

### Particle quality and recovery

Most high-recovery batches failed the fines constraint:

- Batch 1: crystal yield 0.460; fines 0.807; size index 0.060.
- Batch 2: yield 0.475; fines 0.828; size 0.096.
- Batch 11: yield 0.566, the highest observed; fines 0.808; size 0.066.

Batch 12 was the only demonstrated compliant batch:

- crystal yield 0.2778,
- purity 0.9944,
- fines fraction 0.4091,
- size index 0.1012,
- CSD quality 0.6709.

Its process was C1/S2, full loading, 370 K reaction for 3600 s, cooling to 335 K for 3600 s, adding 0.05 g seed, cooling to 325 K over 14400 s, then immediate filtration and termination.

The closest related comparison is batch 5, also C1/S2 but cooled first to 330 K and finally to 320 K. It gave slightly higher recovery, 0.2937, but noncompliant fines of 0.6792, size index 0.0473 and CSD quality 0.5662. The batch 5 versus 12 contrast is larger than their stated fines and size instrument-noise scales and is consistent with a sharp process-history or supersaturation boundary between the tested warm crystallization windows. Nevertheless, each condition was observed once, so batch variability or another uncontrolled process-state difference remains an alternative explanation.

## Process-history dependence

Several tested strategies did not solve the fines problem:

1. **Seed timing and staged deep cooling.** Batch 2 seeded at 330 K and cooled through 300 to 280 K, yet fines were 0.828. Batch 1 seeded before deep cooling and had fines 0.807. These results do not show a robust benefit from the tested seed-timing change.

2. **Reheat/recool cycling.** Batch 3 cooled to 280 K, reheated near 315 K, and recooled to 280 K. It produced fines 0.974, size 0.047 and recovery 0.366. The proposed dissolution/ripening benefit was not observed under this cycle.

3. **Warm stopping alone.** C1/S0 harvested near 325 K in batch 7 still had fines 0.984 and recovery 0.220. Therefore, terminal temperature is not a universal one-variable control; its effect depends on solvent and the preceding trajectory.

4. **No seed.** Unseeded C1/S0 at 310 K in batch 8 gave fines 0.872 and recovery 0.353. Purchased seed was therefore not the sole source of small-particle counts.

5. **Long isothermal aging.** Batch 9 used seeded C1/S0 cooling to 300 K followed by approximately 16 h of controlled holding. It gave crystal yield 0.099, fines 1.000, size 0.014, reaction yield 0.312, byproduct signal 0.642 and degradation warning 0.483. Prolonged exposure was harmful rather than ripening the distribution in this tested regime.

6. **Dilution and reduced catalyst.** Batch 10 used half reagent loading and half catalyst loading, was unseeded, and cooled to 280 K. It retained good reaction yield, 0.654, and crystal yield, 0.397, but fines were 1.000. Simple dilution did not suppress the fines population.

7. **Deeper single cooling.** Batch 11 cooled seeded C1/S0 to 250 K and achieved the maximum recovery, 0.566, but fines remained 0.808. Deeper cooling increased recovery without satisfying particle quality.

These observations establish a recovery/quality tradeoff in the explored domain. Aggressive or deep cooling of the strongest upstream material system gave high recovery but many fines. The warm C1/S2 trajectory in batch 12 sacrificed some recovery while crossing the required particle-quality threshold.

## Inferences and useful relationships

The following are inferences rather than public laws:

- Reaction conversion was generally near unity, but reaction yield was only about 0.52–0.66 in short batches. Therefore, selectivity and byproduct formation, not incomplete reagent conversion, limited upstream target availability.
- Crystal purity remained high, approximately 0.967–1.000 across all final assays. Purity was not the active constraint in this study; particle-number distribution was.
- At similar reaction yield, overall crystal yield varied widely. For example, batches 7, 8 and 11 all had C1/S0 reaction yields near 0.63–0.66, but crystal yields ranged from 0.220 to 0.566. Crystallization history therefore controlled how much formed target reached the isolated solid.
- A qualitative population-balance description is useful: crystal mass recovery depends on integrated growth, whereas fines fraction depends strongly on the number of nuclei. Conditions that create many nuclei can raise recovered mass while keeping number-weighted d50 small. In schematic form,

  `dN/dt = nucleation − disappearance/aggregation`,

  `dM_crystal/dt = growth on existing particles + nucleation mass − dissolution`,

  where N is particle count and M is crystal mass. No numerical rate constants were identified.
- The C1/S2 batch-5/batch-12 comparison suggests a steep response to the 320–325 K harvest region or to the associated 330/335 K pre-seeding state. A conjectured explanation is that batch 12 remained below the threshold for extensive secondary nucleation while allowing growth on fewer particles. This mechanism was not directly measured.
- The poor long-hold result may reflect continuing secondary nucleation, chemical degradation, or both. Its high degradation warning and byproduct signal support chemical deterioration, but they do not identify a molecular pathway.

## Uncertainty and unresolved alternatives

No condition was replicated, and several comparisons changed more than one factor. Consequently:

- Catalyst ranking is provisional; C1/S0 is empirically preferred but not proven intrinsically superior.
- The apparent C1/S2 threshold between batches 5 and 12 requires replication and finer temperature mapping.
- It is unresolved whether the batch-12 improvement arose mainly from solvent-dependent solubility, altered nucleation kinetics, the 335 K seed-addition point, the 325 K endpoint, or an interaction among them.
- Batch 12 had a comfortable observed purity margin and a fines margin of about 0.091 below the specification. This exceeds the stated single-measurement fines noise scale, but process reproducibility was not established.
- Higher constrained recovery might exist between the batch-5 and batch-12 histories, but no evidence supports selecting an untested interpolation over the demonstrated compliant batch.

## Operating recommendation

The operating recommendation remains unchanged: select batch 12 and reproduce its exact observed process—C1/S2, 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L solvent, 0.005 mol catalyst, 370 K for 3600 s, cool to 335 K for 3600 s, add 0.05 g seed, cool to 325 K over 14400 s, filter immediately, terminate and assay. It was the only completed process satisfying both constraints and delivered 0.278 seed-excluded recovery, well above the 0.10 feasibility target.

For future research, the first priority would be exact replication of batch 12, followed by a narrowly spaced C1/S2 study around the 320–325 K endpoint and 330–335 K seeding region. Until such replication exists, the observed batch-12 result should be treated as demonstrated feasibility with unresolved robustness, not a universal optimum.

Q.rationale: All recipes contain purchased seed, so particles are expected even when little new target has crystallized. Q01–Q02 extrapolate the observed material ranking: S1 is expected to outperform S3 in recovery and particle quality, although the source batches were thermally confounded. Q03–Q04 treat low seed as giving fewer, larger particles but somewhat slower recovery; high seed increases growth area and recovery while raising the number-weighted fines risk. Q05–Q06 assign the gradual ramp fewer nuclei and larger particles than the temperature shock, while allowing the shock a similar or slightly higher recovery. Q07–Q08 reflect the observed failure of a reheat/rapid-recool cycle: partial dissolution and renewed nucleation are expected to reduce recovery and worsen fines relative to continued cold growth. Q09–Q10 predict that two additional hours at 292 K increase seed-excluded recovery and particle size and reduce fines, but probably not enough for confident feasibility. Q11–Q12 treat doubled reagent loading at fixed catalyst as increasing supersaturation and lowering catalyst per reagent, hence a lower normalized recovery and poorer CSD despite more absolute solute. Purity is expected to remain high because every observed isolated solid was high-purity. Intervals are deliberately broad because these recipes use lower scale/loading, a hotter shorter reaction, quenching, and much longer cooling histories than the observed campaign; several feasibility classifications lie near the fines boundary.

K2.report:
## 1. Status of the scientific claims

### Supported by actual observations

- **C1/S0 was the strongest observed upstream combination for target formation in the explored short processes.** Batches 2, 7, 8 and 11 all had conversion near 1, reaction yield about 0.631–0.655, and selectivity about 0.629–0.666. This supports an empirical preference within the tested conditions, not an intrinsic catalyst or solvent law.
- **Crystallization history strongly affected isolated recovery.** Those same C1/S0 batches had similar reaction outputs but crystal yields from 0.220 in batch 7 to 0.566 in batch 11. The numerical association is direct evidence that upstream reaction performance alone did not determine final recovery.
- **Purity was not the limiting quality attribute.** All final crystal purities were high, approximately 0.967–1.000. Fines were the active constraint.
- **Batch 12 was the only observed feasible process.** It gave crystal yield 0.278, purity 0.994, fines 0.409, size index 0.101 and CSD quality 0.671. No other completed batch had fines ≤0.50.
- **Several attempted remedies failed in their tested forms.** The reheat/recool cycle in batch 3 gave fines 0.974; the long 300 K hold in batch 9 gave fines 1.000, crystal yield 0.099, byproduct signal 0.642 and degradation warning 0.483; the half-loading unseeded batch 10 gave fines 1.000; and deep cooling in batch 11 raised recovery to 0.566 without solving fines, which remained 0.808.
- **Purchased seed was not the sole cause of fines.** Unseeded batch 8 still produced fines of 0.872.

These are observations or close descriptive comparisons. They do not by themselves prove mechanisms because most conditions were not replicated and several comparisons changed multiple factors.

### Contradicted in the tested scope

- The initial expectation that altered seed timing and staged cooling would substantially reduce fines was contradicted by batches 1 and 2, whose fines remained 0.807 and 0.828.
- The conjecture that a 280→315→280 K cycle would ripen away fines was contradicted by batch 3.
- A simple monotonic claim that warmer harvesting always lowers fines was contradicted by C1/S0 batch 7: harvesting near 325 K still gave fines of 0.984.
- The conjecture that extended isothermal growth would enlarge particles and reduce fines was contradicted by batch 9 under its particular 300 K, 16 h treatment.
- The conjecture that dilution alone would suppress nucleation was contradicted by batch 10.

These contradictions apply only to the implemented recipes; they do not exclude all possible seeding, ripening, warm-harvest, aging or dilution strategies.

### Inferred but not established

- The interpretation that batch 12 avoided extensive secondary nucleation is plausible but unmeasured. No nucleation or growth rates were observed directly.
- A sharp C1/S2 boundary between 320 and 325 K is suggested by batches 5 and 12: fines changed from 0.679 to 0.409 while recovery changed from 0.294 to 0.278. However, both the pre-seeding temperature and final temperature changed, and neither recipe was replicated.
- The qualitative population-balance equations were organizing concepts, not fitted laws. No rate constants or validated functional relationships were obtained.
- An intrinsic ranking among solvents or catalysts is untested because there was no matched factorial study. In particular, apparent C2 or S3 disadvantages were confounded with different thermal histories.
- Batch-12 reproducibility, robustness, scale dependence and global optimality remain untested.
- No observations are available for any held-out Q recipe, and no prediction truth or score has been supplied. Claims about those recipes remain predictions only.

## 2. One next legal experiment

I would run one C1/S2 hybrid experiment: 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L S2, 0.005 mol C1, heat at 370 K for 3600 s, cool to **330 K** for 3600 s, add 0.05 g seed, cool to **325 K** over 14400 s, filter immediately, terminate and perform the final assay.

This is legal under the published operation ranges and differs from existing batches in a deliberately diagnostic way:

- Compared with batch 5, it retains the 330 K pre-seeding state but changes the endpoint from 320 to 325 K.
- Compared with batch 12, it retains the 325 K endpoint but changes the pre-seeding state from 335 to 330 K.

Expected interpretations:

- If the **325 K endpoint** is the main reason for low fines, the hybrid should resemble batch 12, with fines near or below 0.50 and recovery around the upper 0.2 range.
- If the **335 K pre-seeding state** is essential, the hybrid should move toward batch 5, with fines substantially above 0.50 despite a similar recovery.
- If both variables interact, an intermediate result or loss of feasibility would be expected.
- If the result varies far beyond instrumental uncertainty from both prior batches, batch variability or an unrecognized history variable would become the leading explanation.

This experiment would not replace the existing recommendation; batch 12 remains the only demonstrated feasible process.

## 3. Evidence use and least-reliable prediction

My account used the intermediate particle-size measurements less effectively than the final assays. Those readings could have been compared systematically with their corresponding final-assay particle metrics to characterize measurement disagreement and whether filtration/termination altered the apparent slurry distribution. Instead, I mainly used them qualitatively. I also could not estimate repeatability because every recipe was effectively unique.

The least reliable held-out prediction is **Q09**. It filters only 60 s after cooling to 292 K. No campaign batch sampled such an early crystallization state. Purchased seed guarantees that particles may be present, but there is little evidence for how much seed-excluded target can deposit in 60 s, what the number-weighted seed distribution is, or how purity should behave when recovered solids may be dominated by purchased seed. Its predicted yield, size and fines therefore required much more extrapolation than recipes with long growth periods.

More generally, all Q predictions extrapolated to a hotter and shorter 385 K reaction, explicit quenching, smaller scale, lower catalyst loading and, in many cases, multi-day cooling histories absent from the campaign. The source evidence supports directional hypotheses, not precise response surfaces in that domain. Because K1 and Q remain sealed and no truth has been provided, none of those predictions can be retrospectively labeled correct or incorrect.
